personas.summary: Chemistry-first verdict: this is a well-built chapter and is close to assignable. I verified every SMILES (all seven figure molecules plus every question option/card render correctly), the pKa values (alcohol ~16, water 15.7, phenol ~10, p-nitrophenol ~7, 2,4-dinitrophenol ~4, p-chlorophenol ~9.4, p-cresol slightly less acidic than phenol), reagent selectivity (NaBH4 vs LiAlH4), Grignard product classes and the two-equivalent ester case, oxidation outcomes by alcohol class, the tertiary>secondary>primary dehydration order, the halide-forming reagents, and phenol acidity/resonance and EAS behavior. All 28 questions' answer keys are chemically correct against their prompts. There is ONE hard chemistry error that blocks publication: the dehydration/halide nugget asserts that thionyl chloride (SOCl2) AND PBr3 both proceed 'with inversion at the carbinol carbon.' PBr3 does invert, but SOCl2 without an added base classically proceeds through the SNi (chlorosulfite) pathway with net RETENTION; only SOCl2 with pyridine gives inversion. Lumping the two together as 'inversion' is factually wrong and will be un-taught in a later stereochemistry/mechanism unit. Beyond that, there is a misleading simplification (primary-alcohol dehydration described as going through a 'primary carbocation'), one taught-but-unassessed objective (IUPAC naming), a minor NaBH4/LiAlH4 subscript-notation inconsistency between prose and questions, and a real visual opportunity: the three mechanism/resonance video briefs are deferred and hidden, so curved-arrow electron flow (Grignard addition, phenoxide resonance, oxidation levels) lives only in prose. Not-go until the SOCl2 stereochemistry statement is corrected; everything else is schedule-not-block.

location.anchor_text: both convert the –OH into a good leaving group in situ and proceed with inversion at the carbinol carbon under mild conditions

findings.observation: The nugget states that thionyl chloride (SOCl2) and phosphorus tribromide (PBr3) BOTH convert an alcohol to the halide 'with inversion at the carbinol carbon.' PBr3 does react through an SN2 pathway with inversion, but SOCl2 with no added base classically reacts through the intramolecular chlorosulfite (SNi) pathway, which gives NET RETENTION of configuration; inversion with SOCl2 is obtained only when a base such as pyridine is added. Asserting inversion for both reagents is factually incorrect for the SOCl2/no-base case that the sentence describes.
findings.learner_impact: Students building stereochemical intuition will encode a wrong rule (SOCl2 = inversion) that must be explicitly un-taught in a later substitution/stereochemistry unit, and they will mispredict the configuration of SOCl2 products on exams. Because the claim is stated as a settled fact in the expanded reader text, it is high-confidence misinformation.
findings.evidence: nugget-dehydration-halides expanded text / reader block blk-my271ho4: 'Primary and secondary alcohols are converted cleanly by thionyl chloride, SOCl2, to the alkyl chloride, or by phosphorus tribromide, PBr3, to the alkyl bromide; both convert the –OH into a good leaving group in situ and proceed with inversion at the carbinol carbon under mild conditions, avoiding the rearrangements that plague the HX route.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The stereochemical outcome of SOCl2 must be corrected so it is not presented as inversion in the same breath as PBr3. The chapter needs an accurate statement that distinguishes PBr3 (inversion, SN2) from SOCl2 (retention via SNi when run without base; inversion only with an added base such as pyridine), or it should drop the stereochemistry claim for SOCl2 entirely rather than assert inversion.

location.anchor_text: primary alcohols dehydrate only under forcing conditions and are prone to rearrangement

findings.observation: Acid-catalyzed dehydration is presented as uniformly going 'through a carbocation,' and the ch17-fastest-dehydration feedback says a primary alcohol 'would require a high-energy primary carbocation.' Primary alcohols do not form free primary carbocations; their acid-catalyzed dehydration is generally E2-like/concerted (or proceeds only with rearrangement to a more stable cation). Treating a discrete primary carbocation as the intermediate is a simplification that will be un-taught when E1 vs E2 is developed rigorously.
findings.learner_impact: Students learn a single carbocation model for all classes and will later have to unlearn the idea that primary alcohols form primary carbocations, and may mis-draw mechanisms/energy diagrams for primary substrates. The ranking conclusion (tertiary fastest) is correct, so the harm is conceptual rather than an answer error.
findings.evidence: nugget-dehydration-halides: 'because a carbocation is formed the reactivity order is tertiary > secondary > primary; primary alcohols dehydrate only under forcing conditions...' and ch17-fastest-dehydration wrong_answer_explanation for option c: 'A primary alcohol dehydrates slowest by this mechanism because it would require a high-energy primary carbocation.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs a one-clause caveat that primary alcohols do not proceed through a free primary carbocation (concerted/E2-like, or via rearrangement), so the correct tertiary>secondary>primary trend is taught without planting the primary-carbocation misconception.

location.anchor_text: change the alkane ending -e to -ol, and number so the hydroxyl carbon gets the lowest possible number

findings.observation: nugget-structure-naming carries an explicit IUPAC naming procedure (choose the parent chain containing the carbinol carbon, change -e to -ol, number for lowest locant), and its learning objectives and practice_check touch classification but not naming. No question in the 28-item set asks the student to name an alcohol or apply lowest-locant numbering; the classification questions (ch17-classify-alcohols, ch17-classify-alcohols-v2) only test primary/secondary/tertiary and phenol-vs-alcohol sorting.
findings.learner_impact: An objective that is taught in prose (constructing/interpreting IUPAC names) is never assessed, so instructors get no signal on whether students can actually name structures, and students may skip the naming procedure with no retrieval practice on it.
findings.evidence: nugget-structure-naming text describes the naming algorithm; question set (28 questions) contains no naming/locant item — classification items ch17-classify-alcohols and ch17-classify-alcohols-v2 assess only substitution class and phenol-vs-alcohol family.
findings.recommended_outcome: Either the chapter needs at least one assessment item that exercises the IUPAC naming/lowest-locant objective, or the naming objective should be trimmed to match what is actually assessed so objectives and questions line up.

location.anchor_text: the resulting phenoxide can be drawn as several resonance forms that place the negative charge on the oxygen and on the ortho and para ring carbons

findings.observation: The three most mechanism-heavy ideas in the chapter — phenoxide resonance delocalization (video-phenol-acidity-resonance), Grignard carbanion addition with pi-electron shift to oxygen (video-grignard-addition), and the oxidation-level ladder by carbinol-hydrogen count (video-alcohol-oxidation-levels) — are all authored as video briefs but marked production_status deferred and rendered is_hidden with an empty url in the reader. The electron-flow / curved-arrow content therefore reaches the student only as static prose and single product figures.
findings.learner_impact: Learners get no dynamic depiction of electron movement for exactly the steps where a moving curved-arrow or resonance-cycling view teaches the 'why' far better than text: where the charge goes in phenoxide, how the new C-C bond forms as pi electrons move to oxygen, and how removing a carbinol hydrogen sets the oxidation level. Understanding-over-memorization suffers most for these steps.
findings.evidence: topic.package video_briefs video-grignard-addition, video-alcohol-oxidation-levels, video-phenol-acidity-resonance all have production_status 'deferred'; reader blocks blk-74s4t63u, blk-l11ujxt7, blk-ofpvn1qr are block_type 'video' with url '' and is_hidden true.
findings.recommended_outcome: These three steps need an electron-flow-capable representation (curved-arrow / resonance / reaction-progression) equivalent to what the deferred videos would have shown, so the mechanistic 'why' is conveyed dynamically rather than left entirely to prose; the specific medium is for the orchestrator to choose.

location.anchor_text: sodium borohydride (NaBH4) is mild and selective

findings.observation: Reagent formulas are typeset inconsistently between surfaces: the reader/nugget prose writes 'NaBH4' and 'LiAlH4' with plain baseline digits (also SOCl2, PBr3, CrO3), while the question set uses proper subscripts (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄, PBr₃, CrO₃, H₂SO₄). Within a single chapter the same species should render consistently.
findings.learner_impact: Low pedagogical harm, but the mixed subscripting looks unpolished and can momentarily read as different notation for the same reagent; consistency also matters for students copying formulas into their own work.
findings.evidence: nugget-reduction standard text: 'sodium borohydride (NaBH4)' and 'lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4)'; nugget-dehydration-halides terse: 'thionyl chloride (SOCl2) or phosphorus tribromide (PBr3)'. Question ch17-reduce-ketone-reagent options: 'Sodium borohydride, NaBH₄', 'Phosphorus tribromide, PBr₃' (subscripted).
findings.recommended_outcome: Chemical formulas need one consistent subscript convention across prose, figures, and questions.

location.anchor_text: in the presence of water the aldehyde hydrates and loses the second hydrogen to become a carboxylic acid

findings.observation: The oxidation nugget and the short_answer feedback attribute over-oxidation of a primary alcohol to the aldehyde 'hydrating' in water and then losing a second hydrogen. This is the correct mechanism, but it is asserted without the parallel visual/structural support the other transformations get, and the hydrate (gem-diol) intermediate is never depicted, so the 'why water matters' step rests on a single sentence.
findings.learner_impact: Students are told water is the deciding factor for aldehyde-vs-acid but are given no representation of the hydrate intermediate that makes the second oxidation possible; the reagent choice (PCC vs Jones) can then be memorized without the mechanistic reason, which is the chapter's stated pedagogy.
findings.evidence: nugget-oxidation expanded text: 'A primary alcohol has two such hydrogens: removing one gives an aldehyde, and in the presence of water the aldehyde hydrates and loses the second hydrogen to become a carboxylic acid.' No figure or scaffold depicts the gem-diol/hydrate.
findings.recommended_outcome: The hydrate (gem-diol) step that explains why aqueous conditions carry a primary alcohol on to the acid needs a supporting representation or a slightly expanded explanation, so the reagent choice is understood mechanistically rather than memorized.

strengths: Every SMILES verified structurally sound and correctly labeled: ethanol (CCO), phenol (Oc1ccccc1), para-nitrophenol, cyclohexanol, 2-methyl-2-butanol (tertiary), para-benzoquinone, the TBS ether, plus all question-embedded structures (2,4-dinitrophenol, para-cresol, tert-butanol, benzyl alcohol, anisole, benzoic acid).

All 28 questions have answer keys that are chemically correct against their prompts, with feedback that teaches the underlying principle (conjugate-base stability, carbinol-hydrogen count, carbocation stability) rather than just naming the right option.

Reagent selectivity is handled precisely and correctly throughout: NaBH4 spares esters/acids while LiAlH4 reduces them, and the comparison_matrix question codifies this row by row including the protic-solvent tolerance difference.

Grignard product classes are exactly right, including the two-equivalent ester case giving a tertiary alcohol with two identical R groups, reinforced by matched numeric questions (ester = 2 equiv, ketone = 1 equiv).

Assessment set is strong for instructor use: 11 question types across all nine concepts, two variants each, partial credit on ranking/sorting/matching, an error-repair item that diagnoses the tertiary-alcohol-cannot-oxidize misconception, and structure_scaffold draw-the-product items that the chemistry fully supports.
open_questions: Are the three deferred, is_hidden video briefs (Grignard, oxidation levels, phenoxide resonance) expected to remain hidden at publication, or is a non-video electron-flow equivalent planned before the chapter goes live?
Is IUPAC naming intended to be an assessed objective for this chapter, or is the naming procedure in nugget-structure-naming meant only as background context for classification?

personas.summary: The chemistry itself is presented in short, clean nuggets, but a low-confidence student gets stranded in several predictable places: 'carbinol carbon' and 'tetrahedral intermediate' are used as load-bearing vocabulary before or without ever being defined in plain terms; the pKa-to-acidity-ratio jump ('a million-fold more acidic') is asserted with no bridge from the log scale a shaky student may not have internalized; the substituent-effects nugget stacks four new ideas (inductive vs. resonance, position effects, multiple numeric pKa examples, EDG vs EWG) into one dense paragraph with no intermediate checkpoint; the three acidity-resonance, oxidation-levels, and Grignard-mechanism videos that the nugget text explicitly tells the student to 'watch' do not exist in the reader (hidden, empty url) with no fallback description of the frames, so the exact place a struggling student most needs a visual crutch is silent; and no nugget contains a worked example that shows intermediate reasoning steps -- practice checks jump straight from a rule statement to a multi-part answer. None of these are chemistry errors, but each is a place where a student who is already unsure will reread, guess, or quietly form the wrong model and move on.

location.anchor_text: count the carbons directly bonded to the carbinol carbon to call the alcohol primary, secondary, or tertiary

findings.observation: The term 'carbinol carbon' is used as the load-bearing vocabulary word for the entire chapter's classification scheme, but it is only ever glossed once, in passing, inside a longer sentence ('a hydroxyl group on an sp3 (carbinol) carbon'). There is no standalone definition, no labeled diagram pointing to which carbon it is, and no restatement in simpler words before the rule that depends on it is applied.
findings.learner_impact: A weak-prerequisite student who does not immediately absorb 'carbinol = the carbon that carries the OH' from that one parenthetical will misapply the entire primary/secondary/tertiary rule for the rest of the chapter -- and this term reappears as the deciding factor in oxidation, dehydration, and Grignard nuggets, so one missed definition compounds. The student is likely to reread the sentence several times, still be unsure which carbon is meant, and guess when the classification practice_check ('Classify 2-methyl-2-butanol...') is presented.
findings.evidence: Nugget text: 'Every alcohol shares one structural feature: a hydroxyl group on an sp3 (carbinol) carbon. Classification is decided by that carbon alone, not by the size of the molecule.' No figure or callout isolates the carbinol carbon on the accompanying ethanol/phenol molecule assets, and neither asset's alt_text or description calls out the carbinol carbon by name.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs the carbinol carbon explicitly and visually anchored (e.g., a callout or labeled highlight on the ethanol figure) before the classification rule is applied, not just a one-time parenthetical definition buried in a sentence about something else.

location.anchor_text: phenol's pKa is about 10 — roughly a million-fold more acidic than an alcohol

findings.observation: The chapter asserts that a 6-unit pKa difference (16 vs 10) equals 'roughly a million-fold' without ever stating or reminding the reader that pKa is a negative log scale, so each whole unit is a factor of 10. This numeracy step is assumed knowledge from a prior chapter and is never restated here even though the entire acidity narrative depends on the reader accepting this conversion.
findings.learner_impact: A student with weak prerequisites who does not remember that pKa is logarithmic will either take 'a million-fold' on faith without understanding where the number comes from, or will try to reverse-engineer it from 16 and 10 (perhaps guessing it should be a factor of 6) and become confused when it doesn't match. Either way, the number becomes something to memorize rather than something derived, and the same unexplained jump recurs in the next nugget when pKa 10 -> 7 -> 4 differences are used as evidence for ranking questions.
findings.evidence: Nugget-acidity text: 'A typical alcohol has a pKa near 16... Phenol has a pKa near 10, meaning it is about a million times more acidic.' No sentence connects the pKa scale's logarithmic base to the stated ratio anywhere in the nugget or the chapter.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs a one-line bridge connecting pKa units to acidity ratio (e.g., 'each pKa unit is a 10x change in acidity') stated at the first point a pKa difference is converted into a fold-change, so the number is derived rather than asserted.

location.anchor_text: Add an electron-withdrawing group and the phenoxide is stabilized further, so the compound is more acidic: para-chlorophenol sits near pKa 9.4 (mostly inductive withdrawal), while para-nitrophenol drops to about pKa 7.

findings.observation: This nugget introduces, in a single paragraph: (1) the general EWG/EDG-acidity relationship, (2) the ortho/para vs meta position dependence, (3) the inductive-vs-resonance mechanistic distinction, and (4) four separate numeric pKa data points (chlorophenol 9.4, nitrophenol 7, dinitrophenol 4, cresol implied lower acidity) used as supporting evidence -- all before any single one of those ideas gets its own worked example or checkpoint.
findings.learner_impact: A low-confidence student juggling four new sub-claims in one paragraph will likely stop tracking which number belongs to which claim, latch onto the wrong pairing (e.g., attribute the nitro group's extra strength to induction rather than resonance, since induction is mentioned first), and answer the accompanying question set incorrectly by pattern-matching pKa magnitude rather than reasoning about resonance vs. induction -- which is exactly the distinction the linked question ch17-phenol-acidity-reasoning-v2 requires them to articulate.
findings.evidence: Single nugget paragraph packs: EWG/EDG direction, ortho/para vs meta, inductive-only vs resonance-plus-inductive, and four pKa values (9.4, 7, 4, and an implied cresol value) with no intermediate summary or checkpoint between them.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs the induction-only case (halogens) and the resonance-plus-induction case (nitro) to be presented as two separated, sequential ideas with a beat in between, rather than folded into one dense comparative paragraph.

location.anchor_text: Watch the negative charge of the phenoxide ion spread from oxygen into the ortho and para ring carbons

findings.observation: The nugget's own video_brief learning goal instructs the student to 'watch the negative charge... spread... by resonance,' but in the compiled reader chapter this video block has url: "" and is_hidden: true (see blk-74s4t63u). The same pattern holds for video-grignard-addition and video-alcohol-oxidation-levels, both also is_hidden with empty url. The topic package's own production_note confirms these are deferred with no video asset produced.
findings.learner_impact: The struggling student, told by the surrounding prose that resonance delocalization is the single hardest idea in the acidity nugget, has no moving/visual aid at all -- the promised resonance-arrow-pushing animation, the Grignard mechanism animation, and the oxidation-levels animation are all silently absent from what the student actually sees. A student who cannot mentally animate curved-arrow resonance from static prose alone (exactly the population this persona represents) will guess on any question requiring them to picture charge delocalization, since no static substitute (e.g., a resonance-structure figure) is present in the block list either.
findings.evidence: Reader JSON blk-74s4t63u: { "block_type": "video", "content": { "url": "", "is_external": false }, "is_hidden": true }. Topic package production_note: 'Deferred at authoring (2026-07-28)... the molecule-video-creator chalk pipeline cannot produce it... The reader carries the same content in the linked nugget prose and molecule figures.' But the molecule figures shown (mol-phenol, a single static structure) do not show resonance forms or charge movement, so the claimed fallback does not actually cover the need.
findings.recommended_outcome: A required visual (resonance delocalization, Grignard mechanism, oxidation-level comparison) that a struggling student needs to build a working mental model is currently missing entirely from the reader with no equivalent static sequence (e.g., stepped resonance-structure images) in its place.

location.anchor_text: To name an alcohol, choose the longest carbon chain that contains the carbinol carbon as the parent, change the alkane ending -e to -ol, and number so the hydroxyl carbon gets the lowest possible number; substituents are cited as prefixes.

findings.observation: The IUPAC naming rule is stated in one sentence of prose and never demonstrated with an actual worked example (no molecule is named step by step; the two molecule assets in this nugget, ethanol and phenol, are both trivially/commonly named and skip the naming procedure entirely). The one practice_check for this nugget only asks the student to classify (primary/secondary/tertiary), not to name a compound, so the naming rule is never modeled or checked anywhere in the chapter.
findings.learner_impact: A student who is weak on nomenclature has no example to pattern-match against when the compiled question set later requires reading and interpreting IUPAC-style and common names side by side (e.g., '2-Methyl-2-butanol', 'tert-Butyl alcohol ((CH3)3COH)', '2-Naphthol' in ch17-classify-alcohols and ch17-classify-alcohols-v2). They will likely skip trying to derive the name from structure and instead guess based on superficial cues (e.g., counting letters or memorizing common names) rather than applying the stated rule.
findings.evidence: Nugget-structure-naming's only practice_check is: 'Classify 2-methyl-2-butanol as primary, secondary, or tertiary' -- it reuses a name the student must already trust rather than testing or demonstrating how that name was constructed from structure.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs at least one fully worked naming example (structure to name, step by step: identify parent chain, locate carbinol carbon, number, apply -ol suffix) before being handed compound names to interpret elsewhere in the chapter.

location.anchor_text: the tetrahedral intermediate collapses to a ketone with loss of the ester's alkoxy group

findings.observation: "Tetrahedral intermediate" is used as a technical term to explain the ester-plus-Grignard special case but is never defined in this chapter (it presumes a carbonyl-addition mechanism course the student may not remember). The same phrase appears verbatim in question ch17-tertiary-oxidation-error-v2's answer explanation area for a related error-repair question, so the gap recurs.
findings.learner_impact: A shaky student reading 'the tetrahedral intermediate collapses to a ketone' without knowing what a tetrahedral intermediate is will treat the ester-to-ketone-to-tertiary-alcohol pathway as a memorized fact ('esters use 2 equivalents') rather than an understood mechanism, which is brittle: the moment a question varies the setup (e.g., an acid chloride instead of an ester, mentioned in the same paragraph with no separate explanation), the student has no mechanistic anchor to reason from and will guess.
findings.evidence: Nugget-grignard: 'the tetrahedral intermediate collapses to a ketone with loss of the ester's alkoxy group, and a second equivalent of the Grignard reagent then adds to that ketone... The net result from an ester (or an acid chloride) is a tertiary alcohol...' -- 'acid chloride' case is asserted by analogy with zero explanation of its own.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs 'tetrahedral intermediate' either defined in plain language at first use or replaced with a description of what physically happens (addition then a group leaves) so the ester-to-ketone step is understandable without an unstated prerequisite term.

location.anchor_text: in the presence of water the aldehyde hydrates and loses the second hydrogen to become a carboxylic acid

findings.observation: The mechanism by which an aldehyde 'hydrates' before over-oxidizing to a carboxylic acid is asserted as a fact with no explanation of what 'the aldehyde hydrates' means structurally (water adding across the C=O to form a geminal diol) and no figure showing it. This is the exact mechanistic step that explains why water/anhydrous conditions control the reagent choice, which is tested directly in ch17-mild-oxidant-name, ch17-mild-oxidant-name-v2, and ch17-tertiary-oxidation-error-v2.
findings.learner_impact: A student who cannot picture what 'the aldehyde hydrates' means will memorize 'anhydrous = stop at aldehyde, aqueous = go to acid' as an arbitrary rule rather than a consequence of a mechanism, making it harder to recall under test pressure and impossible to extend to an unfamiliar reagent not explicitly listed (e.g., if a question used a new oxidant name they have not memorized).
findings.evidence: Nugget-oxidation, expanded text: 'removing one gives an aldehyde, and in the presence of water the aldehyde hydrates and loses the second hydrogen to become a carboxylic acid.' No structure or gem-diol figure accompanies this claim; the two molecule assets attached to this nugget (cyclohexanol, 2-methyl-2-butanol) do not illustrate the aldehyde hydration step at all since neither is an aldehyde.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs the aldehyde-hydration step (water adds across C=O to give a gem-diol, which then has a second C-H to remove) shown or described concretely, not asserted as an unexplained fact, since the reagent-choice rule for primary alcohols rests entirely on it.

location.anchor_text: Deprotection uses the strong affinity of silicon for fluoride: a reagent such as tetra-n-butylammonium fluoride cleaves the silicon–oxygen bond selectively and regenerates the free alcohol

findings.observation: This advanced-difficulty nugget introduces TBSCl, imidazole (as base), the resulting silyl ether structure, steric bulk as a stability rationale, and TBAF-mediated fluoride deprotection all within one paragraph, with no practice_check step that isolates just the installation step or just the removal step -- the single practice_check asks about the whole protect-react-deprotect cycle at once.
findings.learner_impact: Because this is the last nugget in the chapter and depends on the Grignard incompatibility idea from several nuggets earlier, a fatigued or already-behind student is asked to hold five new pieces of information (reagent name, base name, product structure, why it's stable, and why fluoride removes it) simultaneously with no intermediate checkpoint, and is likely to give up trying to remember the specific reagents (TBSCl, TBAF) and just remember 'you protect it somehow' -- which will fail on the single practice_check that requires naming why a free -OH breaks a Grignard step.
findings.evidence: Nugget-protection practice_check: 'Why can't you add a Grignard reagent directly to a keto-alcohol that has a free –OH, and what fixes the problem?' -- requires recalling the entire chain (proton destroys Grignard -> protect as silyl ether -> remove with fluoride) with no simpler intermediate question first.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs the protect/react/deprotect cycle broken into at least two checkpoints (why protection is needed; how it is installed and removed) rather than one dense paragraph followed immediately by a question that requires the whole chain of reasoning.

location.anchor_text: The negative charge of phenoxide is delocalized onto the ortho and para ring carbons by resonance

findings.observation: This structured-reasoning question is the only place in the whole chapter that walks a student through claim-evidence-reasoning for the acidity comparison, but it appears as an assessment item rather than as an in-nugget worked example, so the student sees this scaffolded reasoning structure for the first time only when being tested on it, not while learning the concept.
findings.learner_impact: A struggling student encountering the claim/evidence/reasoning question format for the first time during assessment (rather than having seen a worked instance during instruction) may find the format itself confusing on top of the content, and may guess at the structured-reasoning mechanics (e.g., which evidence options to multi-select) independent of whether they understand the underlying acidity concept.
findings.evidence: No nugget in the chapter presents a claim/evidence/reasoning worked walkthrough; ch17-phenol-acidity-reasoning and its variant ch17-phenol-acidity-reasoning-v2 are the first appearance of this three-part structure.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs at least one instructional (non-graded) example of the claim/evidence/reasoning structure modeled in the nugget prose before it is used as a graded question format.

location.anchor_text: Although a phenol looks like 'an alcohol on a ring,' the direct bond between oxygen and an aromatic carbon makes it far more acidic and gives the ring a strongly activating substituent, so it is treated as its own class.

findings.observation: The chapter names the phenol-is-just-an-alcohol-on-a-ring misconception explicitly (good practice, matches the topic package's own trouble_spots list), but only corrects it with the acidity/reactivity consequence, not with the classification consequence: nothing in this nugget says explicitly 'a phenol's ring carbon is NOT counted the way an alkyl carbinol carbon is, and phenols are never called primary/secondary/tertiary.' The classify_alcohols-v2 question later requires the student to sort phenol, cresol, and 2-naphthol away from the 1st/2nd/3rd-alcohol framework, but the chapter prose never states that phenols simply fall outside that classification scheme.
findings.learner_impact: A student who has just learned the primary/secondary/tertiary rule and then meets the phenol correction may still try to apply the same 1st/2nd/3rd counting logic to phenol's ring carbon (which is bonded to two other ring carbons, tempting a 'secondary' guess) since the text never explicitly says the classification scheme does not apply to phenols at all.
findings.evidence: Nugget-structure-naming addresses only acidity/reactivity as the reason phenols are 'their own class' -- it never states that primary/secondary/tertiary labels simply do not apply to a phenolic hydroxyl. Question ch17-classify-alcohols-v2 tests exactly this boundary (sorting Phenol, para-Cresol, 2-Naphthol as 'Phenol' family vs Cyclohexanol, Benzyl alcohol, Ethanol as 'Alcohol' family) without the chapter ever having stated the rule the question is checking.
findings.recommended_outcome: A struggling student needs an explicit, separate statement that the primary/secondary/tertiary classification simply does not apply to phenols (rather than only implying it through the acidity discussion), so the named misconception is fully closed off rather than partially addressed.

strengths: The chapter package explicitly names likely misconceptions in its trouble_spots metadata (e.g., classifying by whole-molecule size instead of the carbinol carbon; assuming dehydration ease follows a beginner's naive primary>tertiary guess) and the nugget prose does correct several of these directly with phrases like 'the reverse of what a beginner might guess.'

Every question in the compiled question set carries at least one level-1 hint and a generic_incorrect_explanation, plus per-wrong-answer targeted explanations, which gives a stuck student a path forward rather than a bare 'incorrect.'

The oxidation and dehydration nuggets organize an otherwise multi-case topic around one clean unifying rule each ('oxidation removes a carbinol hydrogen'; 'dehydration ease tracks carbocation stability'), which gives a shaky student a single anchor idea to hold onto rather than a list of disconnected facts.
Terse/standard/expanded text tiers exist for every nugget, offering a lower-cognitive-load entry point for a student who wants the short version first.
open_questions: Is there a planned static (non-video) fallback -- e.g., a stepped resonance-arrow figure sequence -- for the three deferred video briefs (video-phenol-acidity-resonance, video-grignard-addition, video-alcohol-oxidation-levels), or will the reader ship with those blocks permanently hidden and empty?

Is nomenclature (IUPAC naming mechanics) intentionally deferred to an earlier prerequisite chapter the student is assumed to have already completed, or is this chapter meant to be the first full treatment of alcohol naming?
Is the claim/evidence/reasoning question format used elsewhere in the course before this chapter, such that a first-time appearance here would not actually be a novel format for the student?

personas.summary: The chapter's static content is in solid shape for non-visual access: all seven molecule figures carry alt text that names the compound and states the chemically relevant feature (not just 'a molecule'), and the reader renders that alt text as both the image's alt attribute and a visible 'Described as:' caption, so sighted and non-visual learners get the same words. The mechanical answer-leak guard finds zero leaks across all 28 questions, and every option/card that carries a structure_smiles for visual rendering also carries a plain-text label, so a screen-reader user is never dependent on the rendered 2D structure to know what an option is. However, two things need fixing before this chapter should publish. First, the two structure_scaffold drawing questions (ch17-draw-reduction-product and its v2) have no way to be completed without a mouse/touch-capable Ketcher canvas — the question type's own accessibility metadata admits 'keyboard_complete: False' and declares a 'structured_molecule_entry' non-visual response mode that does not exist anywhere in the codebase; the only rendered response surface is an iframe embedding the drawing tool. Second, both of those same questions' accessible_description states the product's classification (primary/secondary alcohol) outright, which hands a screen-reader user part of the reasoning the sighted student has to perform themselves from the reactant and reagent alone — a semantic answer leak the automated id/verdict/number guard cannot catch. Beyond those two blockers, the three deferred mechanism videos (Grignard addition, alcohol oxidation levels, phenol acidity resonance) are correctly hidden from the compiled reader so no broken or silent media reaches a student today, and their authoring briefs correctly specify future caption/narration/transcript requirements — but the reader's video block renderer has no caption track, transcript panel, or any structured field for either today, so there is currently no delivery path ready for when production happens. Finally, the reader's 'Structures and diagrams' personalization toggle removes the entire molecule block (structure, alt text, and prose description together) rather than keeping a text equivalent, which is a real information-loss trap for any user who reasonably opts to hide images while continuing to read.

location.anchor_text: Draw the organic product formed when cyclohexanone is treated with NaBH₄, then aqueous acid.

findings.observation: The structure_scaffold question type's own accessibility metadata declares keyboard_complete: False and a nonvisual_response_mode of 'structured_molecule_entry', but no alternate (keyboard-operable, non-drawing) input surface for submitting a structure exists anywhere in the frontend. The only rendered response mechanism (StructureWorkspaceRenderer) is an iframe embedding the Ketcher drawing canvas at /generator?embed=1&toolbarProfile=lti_drawing.
findings.learner_impact: A learner who cannot use a mouse/touch pointer with sufficient precision (motor-impairment, screen-reader-only, or switch-access user) cannot submit an answer to this required activity at all, even though they could reason to the correct product (cyclohexanol) from the prose.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] sets accessibility=AccessibilityBlock(keyboard_complete=False, nonvisual_response_mode="structured_molecule_entry", requires_molecule_description=True) with the code comment '# honest: Ketcher canvas is not yet (PRD §17)'; the string 'structured_molecule_entry' has no other occurrence in the codebase (frontend or backend), meaning no consuming implementation was ever built. [internal source reference — not in this repo] renders only the drawing iframe with no accompanying text/SMILES/name-entry fallback field.
findings.recommended_outcome: Every learner needs a way to submit a structural answer to ch17-draw-reduction-product and ch17-draw-reduction-product-v2 without operating the Ketcher canvas — for example a text/SMILES/IUPAC-name entry path that the existing RDKit-based structure grader can accept as an equivalent submission.

location.anchor_text: Draw the secondary alcohol formed when cyclohexanone is reduced with sodium borohydride.

findings.observation: The accessible_description states the product's structural classification ('the secondary alcohol') outright. The sighted student is shown only the reactant (cyclohexanone) and the reagent (NaBH4, then acid) and must determine for themselves, from the reduction rules taught in nugget-reduction, that a ketone reduces to a secondary alcohol before they can draw it. The parallel question ch17-draw-reduction-product-v2 has the identical pattern, stating 'Draw the primary alcohol formed when propanal is reduced...' where determining 'primary' from 'aldehyde' is part of the task.
findings.learner_impact: A screen-reader user is told the product class before attempting the question, removing a graded reasoning step (aldehyde/ketone → primary/secondary alcohol) that the sighted student must perform from the stimulus alone. This is a narrower form of answer leak than the id/verdict/number patterns the automated accessibility_guard checks for, so it was not caught by that guard.
findings.evidence: Question ch17-draw-reduction-product: prompt_text says only 'Draw the organic product formed when cyclohexanone is treated with NaBH₄, then aqueous acid' (no class named); accessibility_bundle.accessible_description says 'Draw the secondary alcohol formed...'. Question ch17-draw-reduction-product-v2 pairs 'Draw the organic product formed when propanal ... is treated with LiAlH₄' with accessible_description 'Draw the primary alcohol formed...'. answer_key.smiles for both (OC1CCCCC1, CCCO) confirms the stated class is exactly the correct classification.
findings.recommended_outcome: The accessible_description for both draw-reduction-product questions needs to convey the same task the sighted student faces (reactant identity, reagent, and the instruction to draw the resulting alcohol) without naming the product's primary/secondary/tertiary class, since determining that class is part of what the question tests.

location.anchor_text: Structures and diagrams

findings.observation: The reader's personalization panel offers a 'Structures and diagrams' checkbox (prefs.showImages) that, when unchecked, removes the entire molecule/reaction/image block from the rendered section rather than keeping a text equivalent. Because the molecule block carries the figure's alt_text and pedagogical description as fields on that same block, hiding the image also deletes its text description.
findings.learner_impact: A learner who opts to hide images — plausibly a low-vision or cognitive-load-sensitive reader who still wants the structural information in text form, not only a screen-reader user who would not need the toggle — loses the alt text and description entirely rather than getting a text-only substitute. In nugget-hydrogen-bonding, the ethanol molecule figure's alt text ('...including the O–H hydrogen that participates in hydrogen bonding') is the section's only explicit statement connecting the O–H hydrogen to hydrogen bonding at the structural level; the surrounding prose block does not restate that specific detail.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo], applyPrefs(): 'if (IMAGE_TYPES.has(block.block_type) && !prefs.showImages) return [];' drops the whole block (IMAGE_TYPES includes "molecule"), not just its visual rendering. The default is prefs.showImages = true ([internal source reference — not in this repo]), so this is opt-in and not the default reading path.
findings.recommended_outcome: When a learner disables 'Structures and diagrams', the molecule block's alt_text/description needs to remain available as text rather than disappearing along with the rendered structure.

location.anchor_text: production_note

findings.observation: All three deferred video briefs (video-grignard-addition, video-alcohol-oxidation-levels, video-phenol-acidity-resonance) carry a production_note that explicitly requires 'a closed-caption track and narration that names every meaningful visual change ... plus a text transcript' once produced. The reader's video block renderer ([internal source reference — not in this repo], case "video") has no caption-track prop, no transcript panel, and no structured field for either — it only renders a title, a one-line description, and a 'Watch' link to a URL.
findings.learner_impact: Today these videos are correctly is_hidden in the compiled reader, so no student currently encounters a video without captions/transcript — but there is no delivery mechanism in the reader built to carry captions or a transcript once these are produced, so meeting the production_note's own stated requirement is not currently possible without a renderer change. This is a forward-looking gap on a requirement the authoring process itself already flagged as necessary.
findings.evidence: content/organic/topic-packages/alcohols-and-phenols/topic.package.json, video_briefs[].production_note: 'Production requirement recorded: include a closed-caption track and narration that names every meaningful visual change (electron flow, bond making/breaking, charge changes), plus a text transcript.' [internal source reference — not in this repo] case "video": renders only Badge/Heading/description/Link; VideoLinkBlockContent ([internal source reference — not in this repo]) has no caption or transcript field.
findings.recommended_outcome: Before any of these three mechanism videos are produced and un-hidden, the reader needs a way to carry and display a caption track and a text transcript alongside the video for this chapter's three deferred mechanism animations.

location.anchor_text: Heading as="h4"

findings.observation: The chapter heading structure goes h1 (chapter title) → h2 (section/nugget title) → h4 (every molecule/video/callout card heading inside a section), skipping h3 throughout every nugget in the chapter.
findings.learner_impact: Screen-reader users who navigate by heading level (a common strategy) encounter a jump from h2 directly to h4 repeatedly through the chapter; this does not break navigation but is a structural inconsistency versus a strictly nested outline, and could be confusing when jumping by heading level to distinguish a 'sub-section' from a 'card label'.
findings.evidence: [internal source reference — not in this repo] line 140 uses Heading as="h2" for each section; [internal source reference — not in this repo] uses Heading as="h4" for every molecule (line 179 in StructureCard), video (line 498), and callout (line 390) card title, with no h3 used anywhere in the chapter-rendering path.
findings.recommended_outcome: The heading levels used for figure/video/callout card titles within a section need to follow directly from the section heading level (h3, not h4) so heading-level navigation reflects an unbroken outline.

strengths: All seven molecule figures (ethanol, phenol, para-nitrophenol, cyclohexanol, 2-methyl-2-butanol, para-benzoquinone, and the TBS ether of cyclohexanol) have alt text that names the compound and states its chemically relevant structural feature, not a generic 'image of a molecule' label — e.g. the TBS ether alt text specifies which hydrogen was replaced and by what.

The reader renders each figure's alt_text twice — as the image's alt attribute and as a visible 'Described as: ...' caption underneath the image — so the accessible description is not screen-reader-only content; every reader gets the same words a screen-reader user gets.

Every question option or ranking card that carries a structure_smiles for visual rendering also carries a plain-text compound name/label (e.g. ch17-most-acidic, ch17-acidity-ranking, ch17-fastest-dehydration), so a non-visual learner is never forced to infer an option's identity from a rendered 2D structure alone.

The mechanical accessibility_guard ([internal source reference — not in this repo]) reports zero answer-id, verdict-vocabulary, or computed-number leaks across all 28 compiled questions in this chapter.

The three mechanism videos that cannot yet be produced (Grignard addition, oxidation-level comparison, phenol acidity resonance) are marked is_hidden in the compiled reader, so no learner encounters a captionless or broken video block today; the equivalent content is fully present in nugget prose and static molecule figures.
open_questions: Is there a planned non-drawing input path for structure_scaffold questions (the 'structured_molecule_entry' mode named in the type registry) on any near-term roadmap, or was that field aspirational metadata with no implementation timeline?

When the three deferred mechanism videos for this chapter are eventually produced, will the reader's video block be extended with caption/transcript support chapter-wide, or chapter-by-chapter — and is that work already scheduled?

Is the 'Structures and diagrams' personalization toggle intended as a bandwidth/preference control only, or could a screen-reader user reasonably reach it (e.g. via a shared low-vision profile) expecting text equivalents to remain when images are hidden?

personas.summary: The chapter's seven molecule figures are chemically clean, correctly labeled, and each is tied to a specific learning goal, but they are all single static structures — none of them make the chapter's real comparative and process claims (the acidity ladder across five compounds, the dehydration/halide-reagent decision tree, the primary/secondary/tertiary oxidation ladder, and the Grignard product-class map) visible at a glance. Those four relationships are instead carried entirely in dense prose, and the three video briefs that were clearly designed to show exactly this kind of dynamic comparison (resonance delocalization, oxidation-level branching, Grignard mechanism) are deferred and hidden in the compiled reader, so the promised visual payoff never reaches the student. The fix is not more molecule drawings of individual compounds — several nuggets would benefit far more from a single comparison/summary panel or annotated sequence than from another isolated structure.

location.anchor_text: alcohols therefore have pKa values around 16, essentially the same as water... Phenol has a pKa near 10... roughly a million-fold more acidic

findings.observation: The acidity comparison across the chapter (alcohol pKa ~16, water 15.7, phenol ~10, para-chlorophenol ~9.4, para-nitrophenol ~7, 2,4-dinitrophenol ~4, para-cresol slightly above phenol) is asserted entirely in running prose across two nuggets and is only reinforced by two isolated static molecule figures (phenol, para-nitrophenol) that are never shown next to each other or to the numbers they support.
findings.learner_impact: A learner must mentally hold six pKa values and their relative order while reading two separate paragraphs; nothing lets them see the ranking at once, which is exactly the skill the rank-order questions (ch17-acidity-ranking, ch17-acidity-ranking-v2) later test cold.
findings.evidence: nugget-acidity text: 'phenol's pKa is about 10 — roughly a million-fold more acidic than an alcohol'; nugget-phenol-acidity-substituents text: 'para-chlorophenol sits near pKa 9.4... para-nitrophenol drops to about pKa 7... 2,4-dinitrophenol (pKa about 4)... para-cresol... slightly less acidic than phenol'; compiled reader shows only mol-phenol and mol-para-nitrophenol as separate single-structure blocks.
findings.recommended_outcome: A learner needs a single visual that lines up the pKa values (or at least the compounds this chapter names) on one axis so the acidity ordering and the substituent effect are visible together, instead of reconstructed from two paragraphs.

location.anchor_text: the ease of dehydration is tertiary > secondary > primary — the reverse of what a beginner might guess

findings.observation: This nugget packs two comparative rules into prose alone: the dehydration-rate order (3° > 2° > 1°, reversed from naive expectation) and a reagent-selection branch for halide conversion (HX only for tertiary/some secondary; SOCl2 for chloride; PBr3 for bromide, both for primary/secondary). Only one static molecule (2-methyl-2-butanol, reused verbatim from the Grignard nugget) illustrates any of this, and it shows none of the three alcohol classes side by side or the reagent branching.
findings.learner_impact: The trouble spot the package itself flags ('ranking dehydration ease as primary > tertiary; the order is the reverse') is precisely a relationship-ordering error that a side-by-side or flowchart view would preempt; prose alone leaves the counter-intuitive order to be memorized rather than seen.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json concept 'dehydration-and-conversion-to-halides' trouble_spots: 'Ranking dehydration ease as primary > tertiary; the order is the reverse...'; nugget-dehydration-halides asset_ids is only ['mol-2-methyl-2-butanol'].
findings.recommended_outcome: The reversed reactivity order and the reagent-choice branch (HX vs SOCl2 vs PBr3 by alcohol class) are asserted only in prose; a learner needs these two decision structures made visible, since this is the exact trouble spot the package authors already flagged as error-prone.

location.anchor_text: Show three carbinol carbons side by side: primary with two hydrogens, secondary with one, tertiary with none.

findings.observation: The topic package's own storyboard for video-alcohol-oxidation-levels calls for exactly the comparison this nugget needs ('three carbinol carbons side by side... primary... secondary... tertiary'), but that video is deferred (production_status: deferred) and hidden in the compiled reader (is_hidden: true, url: ''). The two static molecules that remain (cyclohexanol, 2-methyl-2-butanol) each show only one alcohol class in isolation and do not reproduce the three-way comparison the storyboard specifies.
findings.learner_impact: The chapter's central organizing rule for this nugget ('oxidation removes a carbinol hydrogen') is a three-way comparison by design, but the only visual asset built for that comparison is invisible to the student; they are left with prose plus two unrelated single structures that don't show the ladder or the missing-hydrogen contrast.
findings.evidence: video_briefs[2] storyboard: 'Show three carbinol carbons side by side: primary with two hydrogens, secondary with one, tertiary with none... For the tertiary case highlight the absent hydrogen and show no reaction.' Compiled reader block blk-ofpvn1qr has is_hidden: true and content.url: ''.
findings.recommended_outcome: The three-way primary/secondary/tertiary oxidation comparison that the chapter's own storyboard describes is not delivered in any visible form to the student; a static side-by-side sequence (or the animation, once produced) is needed so the 'no carbinol hydrogen, no reaction' rule for tertiary alcohols is seen rather than only stated twice in prose.

location.anchor_text: formaldehyde (HCHO) yields a primary alcohol, a higher aldehyde yields a secondary alcohol, and a ketone yields a tertiary alcohol

findings.observation: The Grignard product-class rule (formaldehyde to primary, aldehyde to secondary, ketone to tertiary, ester to tertiary via two equivalents) is a four-branch map described only in prose. The single molecule figure shown (2-methyl-2-butanol) illustrates just one endpoint of that map (a tertiary alcohol), not the branching logic connecting starting carbonyl to product class.
findings.learner_impact: Two multi_select questions in the compiled question set (ch17-routes-to-tertiary-alcohol and its v2) test exactly this branching map, and a wrong-answer distribution across all four carbonyl types suggests students commonly conflate which carbonyl gives which alcohol class — a mapping that a single reaction-map figure would make far harder to confuse than the current one-example figure.
findings.evidence: question-set.json ch17-routes-to-tertiary-alcohol tests all of formaldehyde/aldehyde/ketone/ester against Grignard reagent; nugget-grignard asset_ids is only ['mol-2-methyl-2-butanol'], which shows solely the tertiary-alcohol product, not the branching relationship.
findings.recommended_outcome: The four-way carbonyl-to-alcohol-class mapping for Grignard addition is asserted only in prose and tested immediately after in two questions; a learner needs the mapping made visible (e.g., a single figure showing all four carbonyl starting points and their resulting alcohol class) rather than one example structure.

location.anchor_text: 2-Methyl-2-butanol, a tertiary alcohol

findings.observation: The identical mol-2-methyl-2-butanol figure (same SMILES, same title, same alt text, same description) is reused verbatim in three different nuggets (Grignard, dehydration/halides, oxidation) that each need the reader to notice a different feature of the same molecule: 'three new carbon groups' for Grignard, 'ionizes readily via a stable carbocation' for dehydration, and 'no carbinol hydrogen' for oxidation. The figure carries only the third framing in its description field, so the first two contexts reuse a caption that doesn't match their point.
findings.learner_impact: A learner re-encountering the same drawing with the same caption in three unrelated contexts may treat it as decorative repetition rather than register that each nugget wants them to look at a different structural feature of the same molecule.
findings.evidence: asset mol-2-methyl-2-butanol learning_goal (used unchanged in all three nuggets): 'The carbinol carbon carries three carbon groups and no hydrogen, so this tertiary alcohol cannot be oxidized but dehydrates and ionizes readily.' This exact text is attached in nugget-grignard, nugget-dehydration-halides, and nugget-oxidation.
findings.recommended_outcome: When the same structure is reused across nuggets with different teaching points (Grignard bond-count vs. carbocation stability vs. absent carbinol hydrogen), the caption/description needs to foreground the point relevant to that nugget rather than repeating one fixed description everywhere it appears.

location.anchor_text: the ring oxygen is bonded to a silicon atom that carries a tert-butyl group and two methyl groups instead of the original hydrogen

findings.observation: The silyl-ether nugget's whole point is a before/after transformation (free O–H that quenches a Grignard reagent versus a protected O–Si ether that survives it), but only the after-structure (the TBS ether) is shown; the free alcohol it was made from (cyclohexanol) is never shown alongside it even though cyclohexanol already exists as an asset elsewhere in the chapter.
findings.learner_impact: A learner has to hold the 'what changed' comparison (O–H became O–Si) in their head from the alt text alone, since the figure shows only the end state and not the transformation.
findings.evidence: nugget-protection text: 'converts R–OH into R–O–Si(t-Bu)(CH3)2... The protected molecule then tolerates the Grignard...'; asset_ids for the nugget is only ['mol-tbs-ether-of-cyclohexanol'], with no paired free-alcohol structure shown in that section despite mol-cyclohexanol already existing in the asset library.
findings.recommended_outcome: The protecting-group nugget describes a before/after transformation (free O–H versus capped O–Si) but shows only the 'after' structure; the comparison needs to be visible, not just the end product, so the reader can see exactly what changed.

location.anchor_text: Ethanol shows the defining feature of an alcohol: a hydroxyl group bonded to an sp3 carbon

findings.observation: The ethanol figure is repeated identically (same structure, same alt text, same description) in both nugget-structure-naming and nugget-hydrogen-bonding, even though the hydrogen-bonding nugget's actual content (why O–H lets alcohols donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the resulting boiling-point/solubility trends) is not shown by this figure at all — the same static skeletal drawing does not depict a hydrogen bond, a boiling-point comparison, or a solubility trend.
findings.learner_impact: The learner sees the same picture twice within two sections without it adding new information the second time; the figure earns its place in the first section (defining the carbinol carbon) but is decorative repetition in the second, where the real content (intermolecular hydrogen bonding, boiling point contrast with propane/ether) has no visual support at all.
findings.evidence: Compiled reader blocks blk-ospbtplv (nugget-structure-naming) and blk-sry0um43 (nugget-hydrogen-bonding) are byte-identical molecule blocks for ethanol; nugget-hydrogen-bonding text discusses boiling-point and solubility comparisons that this structure does not depict.
findings.recommended_outcome: Re-showing the identical ethanol structure a second time does not serve the hydrogen-bonding nugget's actual content (intermolecular H-bonding and the boiling-point/solubility trend); either the repeat should be dropped as redundant, or the visual should instead show what this section is actually about (e.g., a hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor annotation, or a boiling-point comparison).

findings.observation: The phenol figure's description/alt text states only that the hydroxyl is 'bonded directly to one ring carbon' and does not mention resonance, the ortho/para positions, or anything about the conjugate base — yet the adjacent claim-evidence-reasoning question (ch17-phenol-acidity-reasoning) requires the learner to identify that the phenoxide's charge delocalizes onto specific ortho and para ring carbons.
findings.learner_impact: A learner relying on the figure and its description to prepare for the resonance-based reasoning question gets no visual or textual cue toward which ring positions matter, even though the deferred, hidden video was specifically designed to show that delocalization.
findings.evidence: asset mol-phenol accessibility.alt_text: 'Phenol: a benzene ring with a hydroxyl group bonded directly to one ring carbon.' Question ch17-phenol-acidity-reasoning evidence options include 'The negative charge of phenoxide is delocalized onto the ortho and para ring carbons by resonance.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The static phenol figure's description does not mention the ortho/para resonance positions the acidity reasoning question later asks about; the description (or an adjacent annotated figure) needs to name those positions so the static figure and the assessed reasoning are aligned. This overlaps the Accessibility persona's alt-text-sufficiency lens.

strengths: All seven molecule figures are chemically accurate, minimal, and each is anchored to a specific, correctly stated learning_goal rather than being decorative.

Structures are reused across nuggets where the same compound is genuinely relevant (e.g., cyclohexanol appears in both the reduction and oxidation nuggets, which are legitimately linked), showing restraint rather than manufacturing a new drawing for every mention.

The three video briefs that were planned all target genuinely comparison-heavy or process-heavy content (resonance delocalization, oxidation-level branching, Grignard mechanism) rather than being generic decoration, and their storyboards are well specified even though production was deferred.
The chapter avoids overloading any single nugget with multiple figures; most sections carry exactly one structure, keeping visual load proportionate to a text-first chapter.
open_questions: Is there a chapter-level or cross-topic convention (e.g., a shared pKa scale visual used in other acid/base chapters) that this chapter is expected to reuse, rather than building a new acidity comparison figure from scratch?

When the three deferred video briefs are eventually produced, will the compiled reader un-hide those blocks automatically, or does a separate authoring step need to flip is_hidden to false and populate the url field?

Is reuse of the identical mol-2-methyl-2-butanol and mol-ethanol asset records across nuggets an intentional space/production-cost saving convention across all ChemIllusion chapters, or specific to this one — that would change whether visual-005 and visual-007 are chapter-specific issues or a systemic pattern worth raising once rather than per chapter.

executive_summary: Four independent persona reviews of the produced Chapter 17 (Alcohols and Phenols). The chemistry is strong and the assessment set is broad and correct, but three verified defects and one platform-level access barrier prevent publication as-is. Instructor found one hard chemistry error (SOCl2 presented as proceeding with inversion alongside PBr3; SOCl2 without base gives net retention via the SNi pathway) plus a primary-carbocation oversimplification and a taught-but-unassessed IUPAC-naming objective. Accessibility found two blockers: the two structure_scaffold drawing questions have no keyboard/non-drawing input path (a platform-wide structure_scaffold limitation, keyboard_complete=False with no implemented alternate mode), and both of those questions' accessible_description names the product class (primary/secondary alcohol), leaking a reasoning step the sighted student must perform. The Struggling Student flagged the pKa->fold-change (log scale) jump, the under-anchored 'carbinol carbon' term, and that the three mechanism/resonance video briefs are deferred+hidden with no static equivalent for electron flow. Verdict is computed, not averaged: the unresolved required-access blocker (access-001) forces 'blocked', consistent with prior chapters that carry the same structure_scaffold limitation.
consensus_strengths: All 7 molecule figure SMILES and all 35 question/figure structures are chemically valid and correctly labeled (verified independently by Instructor and RDKit at authoring).
All 28 question answer keys are chemically correct; feedback teaches the underlying principle rather than naming the option.
Reagent selectivity (NaBH4 vs LiAlH4), Grignard product classes incl. the 2-equivalent ester case, oxidation-by-class, and dehydration order are all handled precisely.

Each figure's alt_text conveys the chemically relevant feature (not a generic label) and is rendered as a visible 'Described as:' caption; the mechanical answer-leak guard reports zero id/verdict/number leaks.
Every nugget offers terse/standard/expanded tiers and every question offers hints + targeted wrong-answer explanations, giving a stuck student a path forward.

ranked_recommendations.title: Correct SOCl2 stereochemistry (do not present as inversion with PBr3)
ranked_recommendations.need: The dehydration/halide nugget states SOCl2 and PBr3 both react 'with inversion'; SOCl2 without added base gives net retention via the SNi pathway (inversion only with pyridine). The chapter must not teach SOCl2 = inversion.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: A bounded factual correction to one clause fully resolves the error; no new asset needed.

ranked_recommendations.title: Provide a non-drawing, keyboard-operable way to answer structure_scaffold questions
ranked_recommendations.need: Both draw-the-product questions can only be answered on the pointer-only Ketcher canvas; a keyboard/screen-reader/switch user cannot submit, though they can reason to the product.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: Least-complex effective fix is a text/SMILES/name entry path accepted by the existing RDKit grader; this is a platform-level change (structure_scaffold-wide), tracked and not chapter-bounded, so it remains an unresolved access blocker for this chapter.

ranked_recommendations.title: Stop the accessible_description from naming the product class
ranked_recommendations.need: The two structure_scaffold accessible_descriptions say 'the secondary/primary alcohol', handing a screen-reader user the aldehyde/ketone->alcohol-class step the sighted student must derive.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: Rewording the accessible_description to state reactant+reagent+task (without the class) exactly mirrors the sighted stimulus; bounded, no asset.

ranked_recommendations.title: Give electron flow a static equivalent where the videos are deferred
ranked_recommendations.need: Phenoxide resonance, Grignard C-C bond formation, and the oxidation-level ladder reach the student only as prose; the authored videos are deferred+hidden and the single static structures do not show charge movement or the comparison.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: A stepped resonance/структure sequence (or a labeled comparison panel) conveys the electron-flow 'why' without producing the deferred animations; least-complex equivalent.

ranked_recommendations.title: Bridge pKa units to the acidity fold-change
ranked_recommendations.need: 'A million-fold more acidic' from a 6-unit pKa gap is asserted without reminding the reader pKa is a base-10 log scale.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: One clause ('each pKa unit is a tenfold change in acidity') makes the number derived, not memorized.

ranked_recommendations.title: Anchor the 'carbinol carbon' term before it is used
ranked_recommendations.need: The load-bearing term is only defined in a parenthetical; it recurs as the deciding factor in oxidation, dehydration, and Grignard nuggets.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: A clear standalone definition (and, optionally, a figure callout) is the least-complex fix; a full new labeled figure is not required.

ranked_recommendations.title: Remove the primary-carbocation oversimplification
ranked_recommendations.need: Acid dehydration is described as uniformly via a carbocation, and one question's feedback invokes a 'primary carbocation'; primary alcohols dehydrate concertedly/E2-like or via rearrangement.
ranked_recommendations.rationale: A one-clause caveat preserves the correct tertiary>secondary>primary trend without planting the misconception.

ranked_recommendations.title: Align the IUPAC-naming objective with assessment
ranked_recommendations.need: Naming is taught in prose but no question assesses it; a struggling student gets no worked naming example either.
